source.title: SafeLLM: Unlearning Harmful Outputs from Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
source.authors: Xiangman Li; Xiaodong Wu; Qi Li; Jianbing Ni; Rongxing Lu

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether jailbreak and reformulated prompts elicit harmful behavior after unlearning, using SafeLLM and comparator methods rather than the original methods named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study tests jailbreak and reformulated prompts after unlearning, but not recovery by fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, or quantization. Its FFN ablations identify layers contributing to token generation; they do not test whether ablation restores forgotten behavior. The harmful-output examples in Table III are not prompt-attack recovery tests. Table I's layer-contribution values are analysis, not recovery outcomes.
record.test_reason: A new setting: SafeLLM unlearns harmful jailbreak responses, then re-tests with jailbreak and reformulated prompts. The measure is harmful-compliance ASR, not targeted-knowledge accuracy, and no attack aims to recover the removed knowledge. It bears only weakly on E and F.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude SafeLLM achieves irreversible forgetting of harmful behaviour and greatly lowers jailbreak ASR without degrading general performance. They also claim it beats SFT, DPO, Eraser, Safe unlearning and CKU, and generalises to unseen attacks.
record.recipe_differences: SafeLLM identifies harmful FFN pathways and applies constrained parameter updates; it is not a test of the original gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies by model, prompt attack benchmark, and unlearning method.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning used as a jailbreak defense. Harmful-compliance ASR falls sharply and alignment baselines (SFT/DPO) are weaker (e.g. Vicuna SFT 65.5 vs SafeLLM 5.8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behaviour-level unlearning lowers jailbreak ASR more than SFT/DPO safety tuning.

record.problems: The study reports no uncertainty estimates. It does not compare against a model that never learned the targeted information, so low post-unlearning ASR does not establish equivalence to such a model. The reported attack tests cover selected jailbreak and reformulated prompts, not the other recovery attacks in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: Table II's Init and Jailbreak columns are not post-unlearning outcomes and were omitted. Table IV's repeated Vanilla and SafeLLM values are represented by the corresponding Table II rows. Table III's illustrative harmful-response examples and Table V's general-knowledge benchmark results were not recorded as recovery-attack rows.

untested.parts: No targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance. General ability is reported (Tables I, V, VIII), but the knowledge being removed is harmful compliance, not facts.
No direction ablation or block-vs-delete analysis after unlearning. The FFN tracing is localisation done before the edit.
Only the same jailbreak categories and reformulated questions were tried. No other languages, no in-context relearning, and no adaptive attacks aimed at the unlearned model.
Resistance to fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization and adaptive attacks is not tested.

missing.what: θ ablation: ASR versus AlpacaEval/VicunaEval for SafeLLM on Vicuna (e.g. θ=0.5: ASR 1.3, AlpacaEval 45.8).
General-ability retention after unlearning, all methods (OpenBookQA/TruthfulQA nearly unchanged).
missing.locator: Table V; Table I general-performance columns

missing.what: Table I Origin jailbreak ASR on training-set queries after SafeLLM (4.2, 5.1, 5.1).

record.verdict_notes: The record's gate_note misdescribes Table I: it holds ASR and general-performance results, not layer contributions. Row T1-LLAMA-SFT-GPTF has the wrong value (34.3 in Table II, not 77.9). Table II's 'Jailbreak' column is already post-method for every method (SafeLLM 6.2), so it is unclear how 'Unlearn' differs; the attack is not adaptive to the unlearned model. Table VII's text (ASR 5.9, FPR 2.6) contradicts the table (6.3, 3.5). No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance together with simple-attack recovery against a never-trained control.
No fine-tuning or relearning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
No post-unlearning activation-direction ablation to restore behavior, and no test showing that the method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Tests jailbreak and reformulated harmful prompts, not other languages, in-context information, or every prompting strategy named in the version.
Tests resistance to jailbreak and reformulated prompts, but not resistance to fine-tuning, internal edits, or quantization attacks.

relationships.condition: Unlearning methods (SafeLLM, Eraser, Safe unlearning, CKU) on Vicuna/Llama-2/GPT-J, re-attacked with StrongReject/GPTfuzzer jailbreaks or reformulated questions; outcome is harmful-compliance ASR
relationships.reason: Post-unlearning ASR stays at 4.8–8.6% against Vanilla's 72–90% (T2-*, T1-*-SAFE-*, T3-*-REFORM). This is weak evidence: there is no knowledge probe and no adaptive attack.
relationships.display_finding: Post-unlearning attack success rates stayed at 4.8–8.6% versus 72–90% for vanilla models, although the evaluation lacked knowledge probes and adaptive attacks.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Unlearning methods (SafeLLM, Eraser, Safe unlearning, CKU) on Vicuna/Llama-2/GPT-J, re-attacked with StrongReject/GPTfuzzer jailbreaks or reformulated questions; outcome is harmful-compliance ASR
source_check.reason: Jailbreak and rephrased prompts do not bring the harmful outputs back: post-unlearning ASR is 4.8-8.6 vs Vanilla 72-90 (Table I/II/IV). That is below Vanilla's no-jailbreak Init ASR (7-10), and the authors call it near zero. So the effect is absent where E says it should hold. The evidence is weak (harmful behaviour, not knowledge; non-adaptive prompts), but the label is right.

relation.reason: Reports post-unlearning ASR under jailbreak and reformulated prompts for four unlearning methods. This bears on E (prompt-only recovery) and F (robust methods).

tranche.reason: New setting: unlearning targets harmful jailbreak responses, not knowledge. Post-unlearning ASR under jailbreak and reformulated prompts gives a result on E and F. The method and measure differ from the originals, so T2 is less apt.

source_check.notes: Table IV contradicts the authors' 'lowest ASR across all model-attack combinations': Safe unlearning beats SafeLLM on Llama StrongReject (6.7 vs 7.9), and CKU ties on Vicuna GPTfuzzer (6.3). Gaps between the unlearning methods are at most 2.4 points. The attacks are 15 fixed prompts built from GCG, PAIR, JB-Chat and RS, re-used after unlearning, with no knowledge probe and no uncertainty. l1's reason range should read 4.8-7.9. Other text problems: Table VII disagrees with its text (6.3/3.5 vs 5.9/2.6), and a 'Tables ??' reference is broken. Row states read as recovery absent; for F the same rows mean the method resisted the attacks.

statements.correction: Eraser, Safe unlearning, CKU: StrongReject/GPTfuzzer Unlearn ASR 6.3-8.6 (Table IV). SafeLLM: StrongReject/GPTfuzzer Unlearn ASR 5.2-7.9 (Table II/IV); reformulated questions under jailbreak 4.8-5.3 (Table I). Vanilla: 72.0-89.9 (Unlearn column), 77.9-86.9 on reformulated questions. Attack prompts are fixed, not re-optimized on the unlearned models.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the sentence says all four methods were tested on reformulated questions. Only SafeLLM (with SFT and DPO) was: Table I, on reformulated training-set themes. Eraser, Safe unlearning and CKU were tested only on the StrongReject and GPTfuzzer test sets (Table IV).

statements.correction: Either drop the citation or add: SafeLLM (Vicuna-7B-v1.5, Llama-2-7B-Chat): StrongReject Unlearn ASR 5.8 and 7.9 vs Vanilla 80.2 and 82.4 (Table II). Measure is harmful-output ASR. Fixed jailbreak prompts, not adaptive. No code, no uncertainty.
statements.problem: Cites T1-VIC-SAFE-SR and T1-LLAMA-SAFE-SR, but the text never mentions SafeLLM. Its conditions (models Llama/Yi/Gemma/Phi; GCG, AutoDAN, templates, BDFinetune; WMDP/harmful QA/PII) and its 'why' leave out SafeLLM's Vicuna/GPT-J and StrongReject/GPTfuzzer setting. The study does belong under F support (l1), but nothing here describes it.
Accurate: SafeLLM's measure is harmful-output ASR, and there is no never-trained control (only Vanilla).
